Every morning, at the hour when sparrows begin arguing over rooftop wires, a small blue door appears in the alley behind the bakery. Nobody knows who paints it. It has no handle, no lock, and no address, yet anyone who needs an entrance can find it before the city wakes.

The door opens only for travelers who have misplaced something essential. A key, perhaps, or the name of a street where they grew up. Some bring questions wrapped in handkerchiefs. Others carry regrets in jars, their labels faded, hoping the door might return them to the proper shelf at last.

Beyond it lies a museum designed by someone with a playful, slightly troubled mind. Its halls change shape depending on the visitor. In the winter exhibit, snow falls indoors. In the music wing, forgotten melodies continue playing from behind velvet curtains, as if their composers had stepped out for tea.

I first entered on a wet November morning, carrying a watch that no longer agreed with the world. The bakery clock said quarter past seven. The streetlights insisted it was dusk. My wrist said nothing at all, having stopped at 6:12, the minute my father vanished from a hospital corridor.

The attendant wore a coat made of brown paper and examined my watch without touching it. “Time is not a thing,” she said, tapping the glass. “It is a room, and rooms can be misplaced.” Then she handed me a brass tag numbered 312 and pointed toward a narrow staircase.

On the walls of the stairwell hung photographs of rooms that no longer existed: my grandmother’s kitchen with the blue checked tablecloth; a radio tuned to distant stations; a hand-lettered map of streets renamed; and one empty doorway, framed like a painting that had been carefully removed from its house.

At the landing, a curator asked what year I wished to recover. I said 1998, though the number felt borrowed. He raised one eyebrow, consulted a leather ledger, and wrote “unverified” in green ink. When I looked up, the staircase had become a sloping street covered with fallen leaves everywhere.

I recognized our apartment across the road. Its curtains were different, but the crooked balcony remained. A boy sat on the steps, eating soup from a bowl. He looked up when I passed and said, “You’re late.” His voice belonged to my father, though his face belonged to no one.

We walked to the corner without speaking. He carried the soup in both hands, spilling a little with every step. At the bus shelter, he asked whether my mother kept jars of buttons on the top shelf. I told him yes, though I had not visited her in eleven years.

“Ask her for the green one,” he said. “The one with the cracked lid. She called it the moon.” Then the rain began, though the sky was clear. He opened the blue door that had followed us, and I understood that the museum permits only one answer at a time.

Inside, my father sat beside a radiator, older than I remembered, reading yesterday’s newspaper. The room smelled faintly of oranges and antiseptic. He folded the paper and looked at me. “I wondered,” he said, “whether you would come before the soup went cold in this quiet version of the evening.”

We ate together while the radiator clicked like a patient clock. He asked about my work, my apartment, the small garden where I grew pumpkins. I answered, but the details felt ornamental, like labels on exhibits. He did not press. That kindness was the most familiar thing between us again.

Then he gave me the green jar. The lid was cracked, and inside lay a single silver button shaped like a crescent moon. I remembered the jar from childhood, but not the button. He said my mother had found it beneath the floorboards after I left during our final argument.

The museum had not returned me my father; the watch on my wrist began ticking again. Yet something had changed. On the wall behind him, a digital display switched from 6:12 to 6:13, and the whole room seemed to inhale. Outside, birds argued over rooftop wires in the early light.

My father smiled as if he had heard a familiar joke. “The answer can wait,” he said. “But not forever. People forget where they put things if nobody reminds them.” He stood, crossed the room, and opened the door into a bright, unremarkable morning where warm bread scented the air.

I stepped through alone. The alley was exactly as before, except the blue door was gone. In my hand was the green jar; around my wrist, my watch ticked with cheerful precision. Across the street, the bakery’s clock announced quarter past seven, and I realized I had finally arrived there.

Weeks later, I called my mother. She answered on the second ring and complained about the neighbor’s terrible rooster, though we lived in an apartment. I asked whether she still kept jars of buttons on the top shelf. She paused, then said, “Only one. Why? I thought you might know.”

I drove to her house with the jar in my lap. She opened the door wearing her old green apron and looked at the button as though it were a visitor from a country she had never visited. “Where did you find this?” she asked, and her voice trembled slightly.

We sat at the kitchen table, where sunlight made squares on the flour-dusted floor. She told me the button had belonged to my father’s coat, the one he wore on the day. I had forgotten the day. Remembering hurt, but the hurt had windows, and through them I saw tomorrow.

The blue door appears for three minutes each day. Sometimes behind a laundromat, sometimes inside a train station, sometimes between houses where no path ought to exist. I bring questions, objects, and watches that disagree with the world. The museum keeps what is lost, but chooses what should be found.
